name: Chambers's Corinthian Order (overlay on Vignola)

authority.source: William Chambers, A Treatise on Civil Architecture, London 1759, 'Of the Corinthian Order' and 'Of Pedestals'; expanded 1791 as A Treatise on the Decorative Part of Civil Architecture
authority.author: Sir William Chambers
authority.note: Figures read from the Getty scan of the 1759 first edition, pages 32-35, 62, 82-85 and 88-91. The Corinthian is the order where Chambers's text is thinnest and his plates carry the most, so this overlay asserts the least of the five and says so.

module.name: The semidiameter of the column at the bottom of the shaft, divided into THIRTY minutes
module.note: Same module as Vignola - the semidiameter - subdivided into thirty minutes instead of EIGHTEEN. Module figures transfer from vignola-corinthian UNCHANGED; PART figures must be multiplied by 30/18 = 1.6667. One Chambers minute is 1/60 of a diameter in this and in all four of his other orders. Vignola's 18ths give a finer part in the Corinthian than in the Doric and a coarser one than Chambers's thirtieths: 1/36 D against 1/60 D. Chambers's is the finer rule as well as the uniform one, which matters most in exactly this order, where the mouldings are most numerous.

fluting.profile: twenty-four semicircular flutes separated by fillets, sometimes cabled to a third of their height

members.name: Plinth
members.note: Chambers, verbatim: 'The Base is Attic, and its measures the same as in the Doric and Ionic Orders.' ONE base serves three of his five orders. Vignola's Corinthian base is also of Attic form, so the profile agrees; what Chambers adds is the discipline of using a single set of measures across the orders instead of redrawing the base each time. The base is restated here because the module conversion makes the inherited part-values unusable without it, and because the identity with his Doric and Ionic bases is itself the point.

members.name: Upper torus
members.note: Chambers's general rule for pedestal and column bases alike: the mouldings' projection must stay under that of the member above, 'that so the whole Base may be covered and sheltered by it'. He credits Scamozzi with observing it and notes that 'Palladio hath neglected it in the greatest part of his'. It is a weathering argument and Vignola states nothing equivalent.

members.name: Base of the pedestal, with its plinth
members.note: Three tenths of the column - 6 modules - against VIGNOLA'S SEVEN. This is the largest pedestal delta of the five orders: Vignola's Corinthian and Composite pedestals are 7 modules of 18, i.e. 0.35 of the column, and are the two places where he abandons his own one-third rule. Chambers goes the other way and comes down to 0.30, on the ground that the pedestal is a contrivance for raising the order rather than a member of it. He allows one third as the maximum and treats anything above it as an abuse, citing the arch of Constantine, whose pedestals are two fifths of the columns, as the extreme case.

members.name: Dye
members.note: Six of nine. Vignola's Corinthian pedestal gives the die 97 of 126 parts - 0.77 - against Chambers's 0.667. Chambers's base and cap are heavier and his die shorter, which reads as a sturdier pedestal at the same height and a much sturdier one at his reduced height.

members.name: Cornice or cap of the pedestal

invariants.statement: The module is the semidiameter in thirty minutes, not eighteen.
The column is twenty modules and the entablature five - Vignola's figures. Chambers keeps the Corinthian skeleton and reforms the reckoning, the pedestal and the shaft's curve.
The pedestal is three tenths of the column. Vignola's Corinthian pedestal is 0.35 - the one place his own one-third rule breaks - so this is the widest pedestal divergence in the five orders.
The pedestal divides in nine: two to the base, six to the dye, one to the cornice.
The Attic base is one module, identical to the base of Chambers's Doric and Ionic.
The diminution begins at the foot of the shaft, by the conchoid, and is one sixth.

named_spacings.name: chambers-eustyle
named_spacings.note: Chambers's revision of Vignola's 2 1/4 to 2 1/3 diameters, applied to 'the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite Orders' as well as the Tuscan. His reason is a constant ratio of solid to void across the orders: the intervals 'maintain in all of them an equal degree of real solidity'. Note that Palladio's Corinthian is systyle at two diameters - a spacing Chambers explicitly rejects for want of space. The three authorities give three different Corinthian bays and each has a reason.

named_spacings.name: chambers-diastyle
named_spacings.note: The wider interval Chambers retains, and his outer limit; beyond it he counts the order deficient in strength.

named_spacings.name: chambers-corinthian-arcade
named_spacings.note: Chambers grades the arcade pier against the character of the order rather than holding it constant: his Tuscan pier is four modules and a half or four and two thirds and 'his Corinthian only three Modules and three quarters' or four. Vignola's piers are three modules without pedestals and four with, regardless of order. Grading the pier by order is a Chambers rule and it is the reason his arcades read as a family.

derived_rules.note: The upper diameter. Chambers employs one sixth in all five orders and notes that in the antiques the diminution is 'seldom less than one eighth of the inferior Diameter of the Column, nor more than one sixth of it', with Vitruvius grading it by height - a sixth at fifteen feet, a seventh at twenty to thirty, an eighth at forty to fifty. He declines to grade it and takes the sixth throughout, arguing that a degree 'found pleasing' should then be held. Vignola agrees on the fraction; PALLADIO does grade it, which is why the three authorities' shafts differ visibly on a tall order.

Five modules on twenty - Vignola's quarter, retained, and defended. Chambers permits reduction where the order is engaged or in interior work, giving two ninths (0.222) and one fifth as the alternatives he will accept, and permits augmentation to a 'full five Modules' where the entablature must carry more. Palladio's fifth sits at the bottom of Chambers's permitted band, which is a fair measure of how far apart the two authorities are: what Palladio makes the rule, Chambers allows as a concession.

JUDGMENT SLOT. Pedestal 0.3, column 1.0, entablature 0.25: the cap lands at 0.194, about 21 in at a 9 ft ceiling. Under Vignola's Corinthian it is 7/32.5 = 0.215 and about 23 in. Both fall well short of the modern 32-36 in chair rail. In a Corinthian room - which is by definition a grand one - the right answer is usually to hold the classical dado and let the furniture look after itself.

Top width to bottom. Chambers is emphatic that pilasters diminish and that the contrary opinion 'shews very little acquaintance either with books of Architecture' or with the antique. In a Corinthian pilaster order the consequence is practical: the capital's leaves must be set out to the DIMINISHED width, and Chambers's rule elsewhere is that 'the Foot of the Leaves of the Capital must not project beyond the upper part of the Shaft'.

JUDGMENT SLOT. The room as an order, with the Corinthian entablature's cornice taken at two fifths - the proportion Chambers's Corinthian plate carries, and the figure most consistent with a Corinthian cornice of two modules on an entablature of five. 8.6 in at a 9 ft ceiling. This is a judgement because the entablature's internal division is on the plate rather than in the text and cannot be quoted; the range is honest and the point within it is not.
derived_rules.authority_note: Chambers, Treatise 1759, p. 62; the two-fifths division follows Vignola's Corinthian entablature (2 of 5 modules), which Chambers's proportions match.

derived_rules.note: Clear span at Chambers's revised eustyle. On a 20 ft Corinthian column, 56 in against Vignola's 54 and Palladio's 48. The three authorities' Corinthian porticoes are measurably different buildings.

JUDGMENT SLOT. Modillions in the bay, at a pitch of a third of a diameter. Chambers's observation is the useful one: 'the distribution of the Dentil-Band will answer pretty nearly in all the regular Intercolumniations' - dentils forgive a bay that does not divide, modillions do not, and the modillion must land on the column axis and at the corner. Setting out from the corner inward and absorbing the remainder at the centre of the bay is the standard resolution and it is a draughtsman's decision.

conflicts.statement: The Corinthian capital is the most expensive object in the classical repertoire, and Chambers's requirement that the foot of the leaves must not project beyond the top of the shaft means it must be carved to the DIMINISHED diameter - so a capital cannot be bought to the column's nominal size and must be matched to its neck.
conflicts.resolution: Order capitals and shafts from one supplier, quoting the neck diameter and not the base diameter. The commonest failure in a bought Corinthian is a capital whose leaves overhang the shaft, and Chambers names it explicitly as the fault to avoid.

conflicts.statement: At the 6 in default module a Chambers minute is 1/5 in. A Corinthian cornice carries a dentil band, a modillion band, an ovolo, a cyma reversa and a corona with its listel in about two modules - sixty minutes, 12 in - and several of those members' fillets fall below 1/4 in.
conflicts.resolution: Set 9 in as the module floor for a full Corinthian (an 18 in column) in painted joinery, and 6 in in run plaster. Below that, use the Ionic: Chambers's own argument for grading the orders by character applies as much to what the material will hold as to what the building deserves.

conflicts.statement: Chambers's Corinthian pedestal at three tenths of the column is 6 modules - on a 24 in column, 6 ft. Where columns on pedestals flank a route, the pedestal plinths project and the clear width closes.
conflicts.resolution: Set the columns out from the wall face by the pedestal projection plus 36 in, or omit the pedestals: Chambers regards them as a contrivance rather than a member of the order and offers no objection to a Corinthian standing on the floor.

conflicts.statement: A five-module Corinthian entablature is 2 1/2 diameters deep, and Chambers permits reducing it to two ninths or a fifth where the order is engaged or interior. That reduction is often taken for the wrong reason - to gain insulation depth at the eave - and it changes the order's character.
conflicts.resolution: If the entablature must be reduced, reduce it for Chambers's reason (an engaged or interior order) and reduce it to his figures, two ninths or a fifth, not to whatever the insulation needs. Take the thermal line at the wall plane and treat the entablature as cladding.

sources: William Chambers, A Treatise on Civil Architecture, London 1759 (archive.org/details/gri_33125011135288) - pp. 32-35 (diminution), 53 (dentil distribution), 62 (Corinthian column, entablature and Attic base), 82-85 (pedestals), 88-91 and 95 (intercolumniations and arcade piers), 107 (entablature augmented)
William Chambers, A Treatise on the Decorative Part of Civil Architecture, 3rd ed. London 1791 (archive.org/details/treatiseondecora00cham)
Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura, 1562, as encoded in proportions/orders/vignola-corinthian.json
Robert Chitham, The Classical Orders of Architecture, 2nd ed. 2005
notes:
THIS OVERLAY ASSERTS LESS THAN THE OTHER FOUR, DELIBERATELY. What can be quoted from Chambers's text is quoted: the column at twenty modules and the entablature at five ('The Height of the Column is twenty Modules, and that of the Entablature five'); the Attic base with 'its measures the same as in the Doric and Ionic Orders'; the pedestal at three tenths divided nine parts; the eustyle at 2 1/3 diameters; the diminution at one sixth from the foot of the shaft; the arcade pier graded by order. Everything below that level - the Corinthian cornice's dentils, modillions, corona and cyma, and the capital's three ranks - is carried on Chambers's PLATES, whose engraved minute figures are rendered as noise by the OCR of every scan reached, and the Getty scan's text breaks down entirely across this chapter's plate-facing pages. Those members are therefore left to inherit from vignola-corinthian rather than transcribed as guesses. A reader with a clean copy of the Treatise or of the 1791 Decorative Part should extend this pack at the member level; the skeleton and the reasoning are here and the mouldings are not.

WHAT MAKES A CHAMBERS CORINTHIAN. Proportionally it is Vignola's - and Chambers says as much by giving Vignola's figures without argument, which for him is a form of assent. It differs in the reckoning (thirty minutes, uniform), in the shaft's curve (conchoid from the foot, not a cylindrical third), in the pedestal (three tenths, and it is here that Vignola's own third-rule breaks and the gap is widest), in the bay (2 1/3 diameters, with systyle and pycnostyle rejected for want of space) and in the arcade pier, which he grades by the character of the order where Vignola holds it constant.

AND ONE THING WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. Chambers's permitted band for the entablature - a quarter normally, two ninths or a fifth where the order is engaged or interior - is the single most useful rule in the Treatise for modern work, because it licenses a reduction on a stated principle instead of leaving the designer to fudge one.
